haiku-low.q1: Three consecutive breaches (error rate above 2% with at least 500 requests), and no unresolved incident already open for that service and rule.
haiku-low.q2: The breach is appended to the existing incident and nobody is paged.
haiku-low.q3: Resolves after the rate stays below 1% for 10 consecutive evaluated minutes. Everyone with a page_log row gets a resolved notice. A later breach opens a new incident.
haiku-low.q4: Primary is paged at open, secondary 5 minutes later, then engineering manager 5 minutes after that, which is the last level. Each goes by push, with SMS fallback.
haiku-low.q5: SMS is sent if push fails. If both fail, the page_log row is marked failed and escalation continues. If the schedule lookup fails, that level is marked failed and skipped.
haiku-low.q6: Everyone with a page_log row for the incident gets a resolved notice. Pending escalation stops because later timers see the resolved state and drop.
haiku-low.q7: Streaks are stored in Postgres and updated in the same transaction as each evaluation row. What resets them is NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q8: Each instance tries to insert an evaluation row keyed by (service, rule, minute), and only the successful insert continues. A unique index allows one unresolved incident per service and rule.
haiku-low.q9: A 5-minute timer fires escalate(level N). The manager checks Postgres and drops it if acked, resolved, or already at that level. Otherwise it logs and pages the current on-duty person.
haiku-low.q10: The Pager Acknowledge button calls our ack webhook, which records acked_by and acked_at. Later timers check Postgres, see the ack, and drop.
haiku-low.q11: The schedule service is asked at each level, at that moment, who is primary, secondary or EM, so handovers mid-incident are picked up.
haiku-low.q12: It reads the page_log rows for that incident in Postgres, since everyone with a page_log row gets the resolved notice. The mechanism is otherwise NOT STATED.

sonnet.q1: 3 consecutive breaches (each: error rate above 2% with at least 500 requests in the trailing 5 minutes) and no unresolved incident for that (service, rule). Then the incident manager inserts an incident.
sonnet.q2: Each breach is appended to the existing incident and nobody is paged. The unique index allows only one unresolved incident per (service, rule), so a second insert fails and becomes 'record the breach on the existing incident'.
sonnet.q3: It resolves after the rate stays below 1% for 10 consecutive evaluated minutes. A breach after resolution is a new incident.
sonnet.q4: Primary on-call is paged at level 1 when the incident opens. Then 5 minutes later, secondary (level 2). Then 5 minutes after that, the engineering manager (the last level, no further timer). Escalation continues until someone acknowledges (or the incident resolves).
sonnet.q5: If push fails, the same page is sent by SMS. If both fail, the page_log row is marked failed and escalation carries on, and the timer is unaffected. If the schedule lookup fails, that level is marked failed and skipped, and the next timer still fires.
sonnet.q6: Everyone with a page_log row for the incident gets a 'resolved' notice. Pending escalation stops, because timers see the resolved state in Postgres and drop.
sonnet.q7: In Postgres, updated in the same transaction as the evaluation insert. The doc doesn't say explicitly which table holds the streaks. A breach increments the breach streak. The clear streak is the 'below 1%' streak. The doc does not say exactly what resets each streak, only that evaluations skipped for an unreachable metrics store do not change them.
sonnet.q8: Both try to insert an evaluation row keyed by (service, rule, minute), and only the instance whose insert succeeds continues, so there is no double counting. For incidents, a unique index allows only one unresolved incident per (service, rule), so a second insert fails and becomes 'record the breach, page nobody'.
sonnet.q9: A timer-queue message escalate(incident, level N) triggers it. The incident manager reads the incident from Postgres. If it is acknowledged, resolved, or already at that level, it drops the timer. Otherwise it sets level N, inserts a page_log row, queues the next timer (unless N is the EM), looks up who is on duty, and pages.
sonnet.q10: The engineer taps Acknowledge in the provider app, the provider calls the ack webhook, and the incident manager records acked_by and acked_at in Postgres. Already scheduled timers fire later, see the acknowledgement in Postgres, and drop, so escalation stops.
sonnet.q11: At the moment of paging, at each level: the incident manager asks the schedule service who is on duty for that level right then. The lookup is repeated at every level.
sonnet.q12: It reads the page_log rows for the incident in Postgres: everyone with a page_log row for it gets the notice.
